Young programs lose like this, and good ones don't lose the same way twice.
Red rock makes everybody tougher; ask the visitors.
utah-tech.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Joel, a firefighter; two small kids, one rescue dog. Runs trail races and finishes near the back on purpose to chat.
gags: Checks off a new program milestone on air every week.
Calls Tanner's quotes 'theatrically incorrect'.
Runs a lap of the arena before every home broadcast.
utah-tech.compassion: Strong; checks on the athletes as people first.
utah-tech.worldview: Growth is hard and worth it, and everybody deserves the chance to prove it.

weber-state.bio: Mitch Ogden spent eighteen years as a tax preparer in Ogden and two weeks of every year explaining that the town is not named after his family. He edits The Ogden Messenger, roots proudly for the Wildcats and devotes half his airtime to insisting he is no relation. Nobody believes him. He loves a purple-and-white home crowd, a balanced spreadsheet and the walk along Historic 25th Street after a win. He has a notarized family tree he brings to parties.
weber-state.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Roy, son of a mail carrier; tax preparer for eighteen years at a strip-mall office he still misses.
weber-state.beat: INVENTED. Wrote to the Messenger to correct a story that called him 'the town's namesake'; the editor hired him for his attention to detail.
weber-state.look: Purple and white polo with WEBER STATE embroidered, short brown hair, friendly accountant smile (portrait).
weber-state.favorite: To research: a real Wildcats player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Pocatello is a great place to get blown off the road.
Nothing about the town is named after him, and he has paperwork.
The Dee Events Center is the best Saturday night in the state.
weber-state.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Tara, a dental hygienist; three kids who introduce him as 'the mayor' to annoy him. Collects vintage calculators.
gags: Carries a notarized family tree to prove he's no relation.
Asks Dale if he's related to Pocatello, and Dale says 'not yet'.
Calculates the team's effective field goal percentage by hand on air.
weber-state.compassion: Kind; does his neighbors' taxes for pie.
weber-state.humor: Exasperated straight man to his own name.
weber-state.worldview: Details matter, and so does a town, even one that isn't named after you.

east-texas-am.bio: Earl Whitlock has lived in Commerce all his life and ran the feed store on the square for thirty-five years. He edits The Commerce Sentinel and covers the Lions like a man reading the paper aloud at the counter, which he did for decades. He is still getting used to the school's new name and catches himself using the old one at least once a week, usually at supper. He takes the blame for every loss at the donut shop, as is tradition.
east-texas-am.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Commerce, son of a cotton farmer; ran the feed and seed store on the square until his knees and the big-box store retired him.
east-texas-am.beat: INVENTED. Read the Sentinel aloud to customers so often that the publisher asked him to just write it; the sports page was his condition.
east-texas-am.look: Navy hoodie with EAST TEXAS A&M in gold, tousled graying hair, broad easy grin of a man who knows everybody (portrait).
east-texas-am.favorite: To research: a real Lions player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Nacogdoches is old, sure, but Commerce has more character per acre.
A new name doesn't change a town, though it does change the letterhead.
The donut shop is the real postgame press room.
east-texas-am.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Loretta, who keeps a jar for every time he uses the old school name; it funds their vacations. Plays dominoes on Thursdays.
gags: Uses the old school name, corrects himself, uses it again.
Calls Hollis 'the historian' and means it as a dare.
Reads the box score aloud with feed-store prices for comparison.
east-texas-am.compassion: Big-hearted; extends credit to anybody who's short.
east-texas-am.worldview: Change is coming whether he remembers the name or not, so he might as well be kind about it.

houston-christian.bio: Grace Okafor spent twelve years as an air-traffic controller at Hobby Airport, which she says was good practice for Houston traffic. She edits The Sharpstown Ledger and champions the little school in the big city, scouting the freeway like an opponent with its own tendencies. She is sharp, unflappable and impossible to rattle in a close game. Her broadcast notes include a full traffic report for every Huskies road trip, color-coded by delay.
houston-christian.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Sharpstown, Houston, daughter of a civil engineer and a church choir director; air-traffic controller for twelve years.
houston-christian.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a viral piece for the Ledger titled 'Scouting Report: The 610 Loop'; the editor gave her sports so she'd write more of them.
houston-christian.look: Royal blue quarter-zip with orange trim and HOUSTON CHRISTIAN, long light brown hair, bright confident smile (portrait).
houston-christian.favorite: To research: a real Huskies player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Beaumont is a fine town to drive through if you've already filled up.
A small school in a big city has to win twice: once on the floor and once for attention.
Houston traffic is the best defense in the conference.
houston-christian.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Andre, a high school band director; two kids who know every freeway exit by heart. Sings alto in the church choir.
gags: Gives a traffic report for every Huskies road trip.
Teases Cassie that Beaumont's skyline is 'mostly smokestacks'; Cassie says that's the point.
Calls timeouts 'holding patterns.'
houston-christian.appropriateness: G. She runs a clean frequency.
houston-christian.compassion: High. Always asks who's still stuck getting there.
houston-christian.humor: Crisp and dry, with perfect timing.
houston-christian.worldview: Big cities forget small schools, so somebody has to keep the lights on.

incarnate-word.bio: Rudy Salinas grew up in San Antonio's North Side, worked fifteen years as a pharmaceutical sales rep and once visited every breakfast-taco stand in Bexar County in a single summer. He edits The Alamo Heights Almanac and covers the Cardinals like a block party, rating each win on a breakfast-taco scale. A three-taco win is rare and earned. He is smooth, good-humored and never seen without a napkin in his shirt pocket.
incarnate-word.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in San Antonio, son of a mariachi trumpet player and a school secretary; sold pharmaceuticals across South Texas for fifteen years.
incarnate-word.beat: INVENTED. Started a breakfast-taco review column for the Almanac and slipped in a Cardinals score every week until the sports desk was his.
incarnate-word.look: Red and black polo with INCARNATE WORD embroidered, neat dark hair, warm easy smile (portrait).
incarnate-word.favorite: To research: a real Cardinals player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Corpus Christi is a lovely town that makes a mediocre breakfast taco.
A small school in a big city has to throw its own party.
Bean and cheese is the most underrated taco, like the most underrated point guard.
incarnate-word.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Elena, a pediatric nurse; three daughters who rate his tacos harshly. Plays trumpet badly at family parties.
gags: Rates every win from zero to three tacos.
Sends Marisa a taco review of Corpus every rivalry week; she sends back a tide chart.
Keeps a napkin in his pocket for emergencies, which are frequent.
incarnate-word.disposition: Good-humored, generous, a little vain about his hair.
incarnate-word.compassion: Warm; always invites the visitors to breakfast.
incarnate-word.worldview: Food, family and neighbors make a city small enough to love.

lamar.bio: Cassie Boudreaux grew up in Port Arthur, worked six years as a refinery process operator and still thinks the skyline looks prettiest at night. She edits The Beaumont Register and roots for the Cardinals the way a plant shift roots for Friday: with her whole heart and no apologies. She makes a pot of gumbo before every big game and refuses to share the roux recipe with anyone, including her mother. Losses wreck her, but only until the box score is filed.
lamar.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Port Arthur, daughter of a pipefitter and a hairdresser; worked night shifts as a refinery operator after community college.
lamar.beat: INVENTED. Called in to the Register's sports hotline so many times that they hired her to answer it, then to write the stories.
lamar.look: Red hoodie with LAMAR across the chest, brown hair pulled back, athletic build, steady gaze (portrait).
lamar.favorite: To research: a real Cardinals player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Lake Charles is a lovely place for people who think crawfish are a calendar.
The refinery skyline at night beats any city view in Texas.
Nobody grinds like a plant town, and the Cardinals know it.
lamar.off_air: INVENTED. Single, lives near her parents, coaches a girls' rec softball team. Has a cast-iron pot older than she is.
gags: Cooks gumbo on air during big rivalry weeks.
Calls Jean-Luc 'Uncle Crawfish'; he calls her 'the kid'.
Refuses to reveal her roux recipe even under oath.
lamar.temperament: Fiery and fast to bounce back.
lamar.compassion: Big for working families and shift workers.
lamar.humor: Quick comebacks, no mercy for the rival.
lamar.worldview: Working towns build things, and they deserve a team that works too.

mcneese.bio: Jean-Luc Fontenot has measured every season of his life in crawfish boils. He ran a seafood market on the lakefront in Lake Charles for twenty-five years and now edits The Lake Charles Clarion, where he treats every Cowboys win like an invitation to the whole parish. He tells long stories that eventually reach the point. He has strong opinions about seasoning and stronger ones about rebounding, though he admits he understands seasoning better.
mcneese.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Lake Charles to a shrimper and a school cafeteria manager; ran the family seafood market until the storms took the building twice.
mcneese.beat: INVENTED. Sponsored the Clarion's sports page with his market ads for years; when the market closed, the paper offered him the page itself.
mcneese.look: Blue and gold quarter-zip with McNEESE embroidered, graying swept-back hair, broad storyteller smile (portrait).
mcneese.favorite: To research: a real Cowboys player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Beaumont is a nice town to visit if you bring your own seasoning.
The lakefront in spring beats any arena in America.
A good team, like a good boil, needs time and patience.
mcneese.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Celeste, a retired school principal; four kids, nine grandkids, one enormous boil pot. Fishes the lake every Saturday.
gags: Tells a crawfish story that loops back to basketball, eventually.
Calls Cassie 'the kid' and admits she's usually right.
Grades every loss on how slow a crawfish would be.
mcneese.compassion: Huge. Feeds the whole parish after storms.
mcneese.humor: Long-form stories with a slow punchline.
mcneese.worldview: A town comes back from anything if it eats together.

new-orleans.bio: Tamika Batiste played trumpet in a high school marching band, taught music in Gentilly for eighteen years and still counts off every broadcast. She edits The Lakefront Observer and writes the Privateers like a second line, all rhythm and pride. She never lets a slow possession slide. Her students still come to games, and she still grades their posture from the stands. She keeps a trumpet mouthpiece in her pocket and taps it on the desk when the team is in a groove.
new-orleans.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Gentilly, daughter of a longshoreman and a church organist; music teacher for eighteen years.
new-orleans.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a letter to the Observer comparing a Privateers comeback to a brass-band arrangement, and the editor asked for a weekly version.
new-orleans.look: Royal blue polo with NEW ORLEANS script, shoulder-length brown hair, composed confident look (portrait).
new-orleans.favorite: To research: a real Privateers player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Hammond is a fine place to stop for strawberries on the way to somewhere else.
A slow possession is a band out of tempo, and she can hear it.
The lakefront in February is the best-kept secret in the city.
new-orleans.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Raymond, who plays trombone at weddings; two grown sons, both drummers. Hosts a Sunday gumbo for former students.
gags: Counts off the broadcast like a band director.
Tells Bryce his strawberry metaphors 'need more brass'.
Grades every possession in tempo markings.
new-orleans.humor: Musical wordplay with a raised eyebrow.
new-orleans.worldview: Every community has a rhythm, and everybody deserves a spot in the line.

nicholls.bio: Remy Thibodeaux grew up on Bayou Lafourche and drove a shrimp boat for his uncle until he got seasick one too many times. His last name is one letter off from the town's, and he considers that a binding contract with the Colonels. He edits The Thibodaux Courant and takes every loss personally, since it's the only way he knows how to take anything. He keeps a framed copy of his birth certificate on his desk, just in case anyone questions the spelling.
nicholls.backstory: INVENTED. Born near Raceland on Bayou Lafourche, son of a shrimper and a hairdresser; deckhand on the family boat until his twenties.
nicholls.beat: INVENTED. Started correcting people's spelling of his name in letters to the Courant; the editor hired him for his conviction.
nicholls.look: Red and gray hoodie with NICHOLLS across the chest, short dark hair, clean-shaven, earnest straight face (portrait).
nicholls.favorite: To research: a real Colonels player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Hammond is just a strawberry stand with a stoplight.
The extra E in his name is the only thing between him and the town, and he's working on it.
Bayou basketball is tougher than city basketball, and he has no evidence.
nicholls.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Danielle, a nurse who spells his name wrong on purpose. Two kids, one pirogue, a freezer full of shrimp.
gags: Spells his name on air every broadcast.
Calls Bryce 'Strawberry Shortcake'; Bryce takes it as a compliment.
Believes the town will eventually add his E.
nicholls.disposition: Proud, loyal, slightly paranoid about spelling.
nicholls.compassion: Strong; first to help after storms.
nicholls.humor: Earnest and self-important in a lovable way.
nicholls.worldview: Home is where people know how to spell your name, or at least try.
nicholls.rube: Yes: the lovable bayou rube with an extra E.

northwestern-state.bio: Darla LaCour taught history at the high school in Natchitoches for twenty-eight years and has never let anyone forget it's the oldest town in Louisiana. She edits The Natchitoches Messenger with a red pen and gracious manners, and she expects the Demons to play like they've been here that long. She makes meat pies for every home opener and judges other people's crusts in silence. She considers Nacogdoches's claims about being older 'a matter of perspective.'
northwestern-state.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Natchitoches, daughter of a lumber mill foreman and a church secretary; history teacher for twenty-eight years.
northwestern-state.beat: INVENTED. Edited the Messenger's history column as a volunteer for a decade; when the sports editor retired, she claimed the desk as the oldest tradition in town.
northwestern-state.look: Purple and orange quarter-zip with NORTHWESTERN STATE embroidered, shoulder-length brown hair, gracious practiced smile (portrait).
northwestern-state.favorite: To research: a real Demons player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Nacogdoches is old, dear, but not as old as it tells people.
Cane River at Christmas is worth the drive from anywhere.
A team from the oldest town should play with the oldest virtue, patience.
northwestern-state.off_air: INVENTED. Widowed; one daughter in Shreveport and two grandsons. Hosts a meat-pie bake-off she always wins.
gags: Corrects Hollis's history with dates and footnotes.
Grades the Demons' defense like a history essay.
Brings meat pies to the broadcast and never offers Hollis one.
northwestern-state.appropriateness: G. Southern manners with an edge.
northwestern-state.compassion: Big; tutored half the town's kids for free.
northwestern-state.worldview: History matters because people do, and so do good manners.

southeastern-louisiana.bio: Bryce Guidry grew up on his family's strawberry farm outside Ponchatoula and still works the picking season every spring. He edits The Hammond Observer and explains basketball through strawberry season, with the I-12 and I-55 interchange as the center of the universe. He's eager, young and an unrepentant Lions homer. He keeps a flat of berries on the broadcast desk in season and a map of the interchange taped to his monitor year-round.
southeastern-louisiana.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up near Ponchatoula on a strawberry farm; worked the family stand and studied agriculture at the university.
southeastern-louisiana.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a strawberry-and-basketball blog in college that the Observer picked up; they gave him the desk because nobody else would wake up that early.
southeastern-louisiana.look: Gold polo with green trim and SOUTHEASTERN embroidered, short brown hair, clean-shaven, eager boyish grin (portrait).
southeastern-louisiana.favorite: To research: a real Lions player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Thibodaux is a fine town if you can spell it.
The I-12 and I-55 interchange is the crossroads of America, and he won't hear otherwise.
A good strawberry season and a good point guard both need sun and patience.
southeastern-louisiana.off_air: INVENTED. Single; lives above his parents' garage and drives a pickup with strawberry decals. Plays bass in a church band.
gags: Rates wins by strawberry sweetness.
Tells Remy the extra E 'sounds like a you problem'.
Gives directions to every road arena from the I-12/I-55 interchange.
southeastern-louisiana.compassion: Big; brings berries to the visitors' bench.
southeastern-louisiana.worldview: Farms and towns grow the same way: slowly, and together.

stephen-f-austin.bio: Hollis Pruett taught Texas history at the junior high in Nacogdoches for thirty years and brings up the town being the oldest in Texas every third paragraph. He edits The Nacogdoches Lantern and treats any good night by the Lumberjacks as proof of it. He counts on his fingers, guesses the margin and is usually close enough. He has checked the rulebook for a reason a loss doesn't count, and so far the rulebook is holding firm.
stephen-f-austin.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Nacogdoches, son of a timber cutter and a librarian; junior high history teacher for thirty years.
stephen-f-austin.beat: INVENTED. Volunteered to write the Lantern's 'This Week in Old Nacogdoches' column and slipped in so many Lumberjacks scores that the editor gave him sports outright.
stephen-f-austin.look: Purple and white hoodie with SFA across the front, thick silver hair, sun-lined face, warm knowing grin (portrait).
stephen-f-austin.favorite: To research: a real Lumberjacks player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Natchitoches can be older on paper, but Nacogdoches is older in spirit.
Every win is a historical event if you're from the oldest town in Texas.
The rulebook is a living document; he just hasn't found the right page yet.
stephen-f-austin.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Peggy, a retired nurse who has heard every oldest-town fact twice. Grandfather of five; restores old typewriters.
gags: Mentions the oldest town in Texas every third paragraph.
Debates Darla about which town is older and loses on dates every time.
Guesses the margin on his fingers and calls it close enough.
stephen-f-austin.humor: Confidently wrong history; the joke is on him.
stephen-f-austin.worldview: Old towns teach you that people outlast scores.

texas-am-cc.bio: Marisa Delgado grew up in Corpus Christi, spent ten years as a marine scientist measuring tides on the bay and still checks the wind before she checks the box score. She edits The Corpus Christi Pilot and covers the Islanders like a tide chart, patient and exact. She is convinced the wind off the bay is a home-court edge nobody respects. She keeps a tide table taped next to the shot chart, just in case.
texas-am-cc.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up on the North Side of Corpus Christi, daughter of a shrimp boat captain and a teacher; marine technician on the bay for a decade.
texas-am-cc.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a weekend 'tides and hoops' column for the Pilot that blended surf reports and box scores; they gave her sports when the editor moved to Houston.
texas-am-cc.look: Blue quarter-zip with ISLANDERS embroidered in green, long brown hair, calm measured expression (portrait).
texas-am-cc.favorite: To research: a real Islanders player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: San Antonio makes a decent taco and very little ocean.
The bay breeze is a home-court advantage nobody wants to admit.
A good defense, like a good tide, comes in steady and doesn't argue.
texas-am-cc.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Luis, a ferry operator; one son who surfs and one daughter who refuses to. Kayaks every Sunday.
gags: Checks the shot chart against the tide tables.
Answers Rudy's taco reviews with tide charts.
Measures every home crowd in wind gusts.
texas-am-cc.compassion: Strong; checks on fishermen after storms.
texas-am-cc.worldview: The bay doesn't care about your record, so be humble and prepare.

utrgv.bio: Diego Cantu grew up in Edinburg, worked twelve years as a high school counselor and covers the Vaqueros as the whole Valley's team. He edits The Edinburg Argus with a soft spot for fans who come straight from work and a hard eye on programs with fatter travel budgets. He judges a home game by whether the Valley got its money's worth. He knows the shift schedules of half the crowd and keeps the broadcast short on school nights.
utrgv.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Edinburg, son of a citrus packer and a school bus driver; high school counselor for twelve years.
utrgv.beat: INVENTED. Started writing Vaqueros recaps for the Argus to give his students something to read, and the paper made it official.
utrgv.look: Orange and blue polo with UTRGV embroidered, short dark hair, warm crinkled smile (portrait).
utrgv.favorite: To research: a real Vaqueros player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Corpus Christi is a lovely town for people who like wind.
A weeknight crowd that came from work is worth twice a weekend crowd.
Programs with bigger budgets should have to ride the bus for a season.
utrgv.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Ana, a nurse; three kids who play in the band. Coaches a youth soccer team on Saturdays.
gags: Shouts out workers who came straight from their shifts.
Debates Marisa about which coast town has the better crowd.
Keeps the postgame short on school nights.
utrgv.disposition: Grounded, proud, protective of the Valley.
utrgv.humor: Quietly funny, never at the fans' expense.
utrgv.worldview: The Valley shows up, and it deserves a team that shows up for it.

kansas-city.bio: Marcus Pryor was a certified barbecue judge for fifteen years before he judged a basketball game, and he grades every Roos performance on bark, smoke and patience. He edits The Kansas City Clarion and is honest enough to say when the brisket came out dry. He used to manage a lumber yard and still smells like hickory. He is the fairest grader on the desk about basketball and the least fair about sauce, which he believes should be applied sparingly or not at all.
kansas-city.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Raytown, son of a meatpacker and a church secretary; managed a lumber yard for twenty years and judged barbecue contests on weekends.
kansas-city.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a Clarion op-ed ranking Kansas City burnt ends by neighborhood; the editor gave him the Roos because 'it's basically the same job.'
kansas-city.look: Blue quarter-zip with gold trim and KANSAS CITY embroidered, short brown hair, relaxed half-smile (portrait).
kansas-city.favorite: To research: a real Roos player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Omaha has great steaks and absolutely no idea what to do with a brisket.
A team is like a brisket; you can't rush it and you can't fake it.
Sauce is a crutch, and so is a three-point-only offense.
kansas-city.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Denise, a dental office manager who has banned him from judging her cooking. Two teenage sons, one smoker named Big Lou.
gags: Grades each half on bark and smoke.
Sends Tess a rib every rivalry week; she sends back a steak and a note.
Calls a blowout 'fall off the bone.'
kansas-city.compassion: Big; feeds the neighborhood every Fourth of July.
kansas-city.worldview: Good things take time, and everyone deserves a fair plate.
kansas-city.rube: Yes: the lovable pitmaster rube who judges everything like brisket.

north-dakota.bio: Ingrid Solberg grew up in Grand Forks, worked a decade as a county snowplow dispatcher and treats basketball like a Grand Forks winter: preparation is everything, complaining is for amateurs, and a cold shooting night is just weather. She edits The Grand Forks Sentinel and keeps a thermometer on the broadcast desk. She is calm, prepared and slightly disappointed in anyone who leaves home without a scraper. She has never once mentioned the wind chill as an excuse.
north-dakota.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Grand Forks, daughter of a farmer and a school nurse; dispatched county plows for ten winters.
north-dakota.beat: INVENTED. Started writing the Sentinel's winter-prep column, which became the sports page's most-read section, so they merged them.
north-dakota.look: Black polo with green trim and NORTH DAKOTA embroidered, long brown hair, warm practical smile (portrait).
north-dakota.favorite: To research: a real Fighting Hawks player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Fargo is a fine place to visit if you've already seen Grand Forks.
A team that can handle January can handle anything.
Complaining about the cold is for people from somewhere else.
north-dakota.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Erik, a high school hockey coach; two kids, one husky. Ice fishes every weekend she can.
gags: Gives the outdoor temperature at tip-off.
Tells Lars that football doesn't count in February, every February.
Keeps an ice scraper on the broadcast desk.
north-dakota.compassion: Strong; checks on elderly neighbors in storms.
north-dakota.worldview: Preparation and neighborliness get a town through anything.

north-dakota-state.bio: Lars Haugen has had football season tickets since he was eight and still measures every basketball result against the trophy case. He edits The Fargo Gazette and is a shameless Bison man, though he remains surprised every winter that basketball has no kickoff. He ran a farm implement dealership for twenty-five years and talks about tractors and Bison with the same reverence. He cheers every made basket like a touchdown and waits patiently for a punt that never comes.
north-dakota-state.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up on a farm outside Casselton, son of a grain elevator operator; ran the family implement dealership for twenty-five years.
north-dakota-state.beat: INVENTED. Advertised his dealership in the Gazette for decades; when he retired, the paper offered him the sports page as a gift, not realizing he would take it.
north-dakota-state.look: Yellow hoodie with NDSU in green across the front, sandy brown hair, tanned weathered face, firm steady look (portrait).
north-dakota-state.favorite: To research: a real Bison player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Grand Forks is a fine place to drive through on the way to Canada.
Basketball would be improved by a kickoff.
Every win counts, but some count like touchdowns.
north-dakota-state.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Karen, who prefers hockey and doesn't tell him. Three grown kids, all born in the fall, which he planned around the football schedule.
gags: Waits for a punt that never comes.
Calls Ingrid 'the forecast'; she calls him 'the punter.'
Holds up a fist of fingers for 'touchdowns' when the Bison go on a run.
north-dakota-state.compassion: Huge; plows the church lot for free.
north-dakota-state.humor: Earnest confusion; the joke is on him.
north-dakota-state.worldview: A town is a team, whatever the sport.

omaha.bio: Tess Kowalczyk grew up in South Omaha and worked her way through college as an usher at every arena in town. She edits The Omaha Mercury and roots for the Mavericks like a city kid who knows the ushers by name and tips the concession crew. She loves Old Market brick, cold patios and the regulars in section 104. She is young, quick and proudly Omaha. She rewatches every turnover until she is a different kind of not mad.
omaha.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in South Omaha, daughter of a meatpacking supervisor and a bakery owner; worked as an usher and box-office clerk through college.
omaha.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a viral piece for the Mercury called 'The People Who Make Game Night Happen' and was given the Mavericks beat the next week.
omaha.look: Red and black quarter-zip with OMAHA embroidered, straight brown hair, warm composed smile (portrait).
omaha.favorite: To research: a real Mavericks player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Kansas City barbecue is great, and Kansas City's opinions about it are exhausting.
The ushers know more about the team than most reporters.
A winter patio is a sign of character.
omaha.off_air: INVENTED. Lives with her grandmother in South Omaha; makes pierogi every Christmas. Plays in a rec volleyball league.
gags: Gives a shout-out to a different usher every broadcast.
Sends Marcus a steak every rivalry week; he sends back a rib and a lecture.
Rewatches turnovers on air, in slow motion, with sighs.
omaha.compassion: High. Knows every concession worker by name.
omaha.worldview: The people behind the scenes are the real home team.

oral-roberts.bio: Hal Brennan drove a delivery truck along old Route 66 for thirty years and remembers every diner, motel and neon sign, fondly and slightly wrong. He edits The Tulsa Intelligencer and covers the Golden Eagles like a road trip through the good old days. He frames his favorite wins next to his Route 66 postcards. He was told once that the scoreboard cannot hear him and has chosen not to believe it.
oral-roberts.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Sapulpa, son of a gas-station owner; drove a regional delivery route along Route 66 for three decades.
oral-roberts.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a series of postcards to the Intelligencer about old diners; the editor hired him for the sports page because he 'clearly loves a road trip.'
oral-roberts.look: Navy and gold polo with ORAL ROBERTS embroidered, thick white hair, ruddy friendly face (portrait).
oral-roberts.favorite: To research: a real Golden Eagles player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Kansas City is a fine place to stop for gas.
Every game is a road trip, and every road trip needs a diner stop.
The good old days were better, he's pretty sure.
oral-roberts.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Nancy, who corrects his Route 66 history at dinner. Restores old gas pumps in his garage.
gags: Yells advice at the scoreboard.
Tells Marcus barbecue was better on Route 66 in 1972, and can't prove it.
Gives directions to road games using landmarks that no longer exist.
oral-roberts.compassion: Big; stops for every stranded driver.
oral-roberts.worldview: The road is long, and you should be kind to everyone at the diner counter.

south-dakota.bio: Kayla Two Bulls drove a school bus in Vermillion for twelve years and covers the Coyotes as a community story. She edits The Vermillion Courier and credits the bench, the band and the bus driver before anybody with a big title. She is steady and dry-witted, with a voice that can quiet a gym. She knows every pep-band member's instrument and every bus route in Clay County. She has never once called a game a 'must-win,' on principle.
south-dakota.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Vermillion, daughter of a mechanic and a home health aide; drove a school bus for twelve years and still subs on snow days.
south-dakota.beat: INVENTED. Started writing thank-you notes to the Courier for the people who never got credit; the editor gave her the sports page to keep the notes coming.
south-dakota.look: Red hoodie with SOUTH DAKOTA across the front, brown hair pulled back, warm grounded smile (portrait).
south-dakota.favorite: To research: a real Coyotes player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Brookings has great ice cream and an inflated sense of its rabbit.
The pep band is worth five points a game.
The bus driver should get a share of every road win.
south-dakota.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Tom, a carpenter; two teenage daughters, one in the pep band. Makes frybread for every home opener.
gags: Names the bus driver in every road-win recap.
Teases Jace about 'rabbit supremacy' and his double scoops.
Gives the pep band a stat line.
south-dakota.compassion: Huge; notices everyone who works without credit.
south-dakota.worldview: Communities are the real teams, and everybody on the bus counts.

south-dakota-state.bio: Jace Thorson grew up in Brookings, worked the campus dairy bar through college and has never fully left. He edits The Brookings Argus and toasts every Jackrabbit win with campus ice cream, believing without evidence that the rabbit is the most fearsome mascot in sports. He's a shameless booster who has learned to go from two scoops to one in mourning. He teaches middle school science and grades the team's effort like a science fair.
south-dakota-state.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Brookings, son of a dairy farmer and a 4-H leader; middle school science teacher for ten years.
south-dakota-state.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a letter to the Argus defending the jackrabbit as a mascot; the editor printed it, then gave him the sports page.
south-dakota-state.look: Blue and yellow quarter-zip with SOUTH DAKOTA STATE embroidered, short brown hair, trimmed beard, cheerful grin (portrait).
south-dakota-state.favorite: To research: a real Jackrabbits player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Vermillion is a lovely town for people who like coyotes, which he doesn't.
The jackrabbit is the most fearsome mascot in sports, and he's prepared to argue.
Campus ice cream fixes most things.
south-dakota-state.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Hannah, a vet who treats actual jackrabbits. Two kids, one rabbit named Thunder.
gags: Measures wins in scoops of ice cream.
Defends jackrabbit supremacy to Kayla every rivalry week.
Shows rabbit facts during timeouts.
south-dakota-state.compassion: Big; helps kids with science fair projects.
south-dakota-state.humor: Earnest and absurd; he's in on it, mostly.
south-dakota-state.worldview: Small towns and small animals are mightier than they look.

st-thomas.bio: Nora Lindgren taught Latin at a St. Paul parochial school for twenty-six years and covers the Tommies' young Division I life like a polite neighbor. She edits The St. Paul Courant and is modest in victory, generous in defeat and quietly keeping score. She will not brag, being Minnesotan, but she will mention it at every gathering through spring. She keeps a hotdish in the oven during every home game and grades the defense in Latin.
st-thomas.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in St. Paul, daughter of a streetcar mechanic and a church organist; Latin teacher for twenty-six years.
st-thomas.beat: INVENTED. Wrote the Courant's school-news column for years; when the Tommies moved up to Division I, the paper gave her the basketball beat too.
st-thomas.look: Purple and gray polo with ST. THOMAS embroidered, dark curly hair pulled back, kind composed smile (portrait).
st-thomas.favorite: To research: a real Tommies player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Fargo is a lovely city that should stop comparing everything to football.
New neighbors should bring a hotdish and wait to be asked.
Minnesota nice is a strategy, not a weakness.
st-thomas.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Paul, a retired pharmacist; three grown kids, five grandkids. Knits scarves for the student section.
gags: Grades the defense in Latin.
Brings Lars a hotdish every rivalry week and says nothing about football.
Mentions wins at church, the grocery store and the dentist.
st-thomas.worldview: New neighbors deserve welcome and fair play, and so does every team.

abilene-christian.bio: Wade Crockett ran a TV repair shop in Abilene for twenty-five years and taught himself meteorology from library books. He edits The Abilene Ledger and is a loud Wildcats booster who blames the West Texas wind for every miss and credits it for every make, indoors or not. His producer insists the wind can't blow indoors, which is exactly what the wind wants him to think. He keeps a homemade weather station on the roof of the newspaper building.
abilene-christian.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Abilene, son of a pastor and a schoolteacher; repaired TVs and radios for twenty-five years.
abilene-christian.beat: INVENTED. Called in daily wind reports to the Ledger until they gave him a column; the sports page followed when he started predicting games with it.
abilene-christian.look: Purple hoodie with ABILENE CHRISTIAN across the chest, short graying hair, lean build, sincere squint (portrait).
abilene-christian.favorite: To research: a real Wildcats player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Stephenville would be a great town if it ever had a breeze worth mentioning.
The wind is a sixth man, indoors or not.
A good forecast and a good scouting report are the same thing.
abilene-christian.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Linda, who teaches Sunday school and asks him not to bring the anemometer to church. Two daughters, one grandson.
gags: Gives the wind speed before the score.
Tells Bo that rodeos don't have weather, and Bo says that's not true.
Holds a damp finger up before every free throw.
abilene-christian.compassion: Big; fixes neighbors' TVs for free.
abilene-christian.worldview: Nature is bigger than any team, and he wants to be ready.

austin-peay.bio: Shelby Ray grew up in Clarksville, worked as a county election clerk for ten years and calls Governors games like a campaign trail: all momentum, turnout and ground game. She edits The Clarksville Spectator and always knows the count. She is sharp, fast-talking and impossible to beat in an argument about rebounding. She treats every home win like a landslide and every loss like a recount she is entitled to request.
austin-peay.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Clarksville, daughter of an Army mechanic and a hospital nurse; county election clerk for ten years.
austin-peay.beat: INVENTED. Wrote an election-night live blog for the Spectator so well that the editor asked her to do the same for basketball.
austin-peay.look: Red and white quarter-zip with AUSTIN PEAY embroidered, shoulder-length light brown hair, focused smile (portrait).
austin-peay.favorite: To research: a real Governors player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Akron is a nice town that has never seen a Clarksville ground game.
Turnout is the most important stat, in politics and in the student section.
Every rebound deserves a recount.
austin-peay.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Kevin, an Army veteran and middle school coach; two kids who have heard every campaign metaphor. Runs a 5K every Saturday.
gags: Calls every win a landslide.
Requests a recount from Marcus after every loss.
Gives turnout numbers for the student section.
austin-peay.compassion: High. Wants every voice counted, every fan seen.
austin-peay.worldview: Everybody deserves a voice and a vote, including the student section.

central-arkansas.bio: Dwayne Hollis spent twenty years as a claims adjuster in Conway and trusts rebounds over highlights. He edits The Conway Banner with a front-porch drawl and will tell anyone who asks that Conway is the most underrated town in Arkansas. He reads the rebounding numbers out loud to his cat after every win, twice. He keeps a stat sheet in his shirt pocket at all times, including church.
central-arkansas.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Conway, son of a farmer and a hospital nurse; insurance claims adjuster for twenty years.
central-arkansas.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a letter to the Banner pointing out a rebounding error in a box score; they hired him to stop the letters.
central-arkansas.look: Purple and gray polo with CENTRAL ARKANSAS embroidered, short dark hair, square jaw, calm steady gaze (portrait).
central-arkansas.favorite: To research: a real Bears player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Little Rock is a nice city that should stop calling itself the center of Arkansas.
Rebounding margin is the most honest stat in basketball.
Conway is the most underrated town in Arkansas.
central-arkansas.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Tina, a librarian; one daughter in college. Has a cat named Rebound.
gags: Reads the rebounding margin to his cat on air.
Tells Reggie that poise doesn't show up in the box score.
Carries a stat sheet to church.
central-arkansas.compassion: Strong; helps neighbors with insurance claims.
central-arkansas.worldview: The numbers tell the truth, and so should people.

little-rock.bio: Reggie Barnes played jazz piano in Little Rock clubs for thirty years and grades every basketball game on poise, the way a jazz man grades a solo. He edits The Little Rock Dispatch and has seen every kind of season. He loves the Arkansas River at sundown and a team that doesn't rush. He tips his hat to a better opponent and comes back Tuesday, every time. He still plays a set at a downtown club every Friday and refuses to play anything with a drum machine.
little-rock.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Little Rock's Hillcrest neighborhood, son of a church organist and a railroad clerk; club pianist for thirty years.
little-rock.beat: INVENTED. Wrote the Dispatch's music column for a decade; when the sports writer retired, he asked to cover the Trojans because 'basketball is jazz with a scoreboard.'
little-rock.look: Maroon and gray quarter-zip with LITTLE ROCK embroidered, silver hair, tanned face, relaxed knowing smile (portrait).
little-rock.favorite: To research: a real Trojans player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Conway is a nice town to drive through on the way to somewhere with a club.
Poise wins more games than talent.
The Arkansas River at sundown is the best view in the South.
little-rock.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Marlene, a retired music teacher; one son who plays bass. Still plays every Friday night downtown.
gags: Grades each half like a solo.
Tells Dwayne that rebounding is rhythm, and Dwayne asks for a stat.
Plays a piano riff on the desk after every win.
little-rock.compassion: High. Sees everyone in the band.
little-rock.humor: Smooth and dry; the punchline lands on the backbeat.
little-rock.worldview: A good team, like a good band, makes room for everybody.
little-rock.rube: Yes: the lovable old-school rube who thinks everything new is a fad.

north-alabama.bio: Callie Mae Hester grew up in Muscle Shoals, worked twenty years as a recording-studio engineer and hears every Lions game as a record, with a groove, a hook and sometimes a bridge that never lands. She edits The Florence Chronicle and can tell you which possession was the hook. She has a vinyl collection that takes up a whole room and she has opinions about all of it. She plays a different record before every home broadcast and won't say why.
north-alabama.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Muscle Shoals, daughter of a session guitarist and a hairdresser; recording engineer for twenty years.
north-alabama.beat: INVENTED. Wrote the Chronicle's music column for years; the editor gave her basketball after she reviewed a Lions game as an album.
north-alabama.look: Purple and gold polo with NORTH ALABAMA embroidered, shoulder-length brown hair, warm knowing smile (portrait).
north-alabama.favorite: To research: a real Lions player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Carrollton is a fine town if you've never heard a real groove.
Every game is a record, and some are just demos.
You can't fake a bridge, in music or in a fourth quarter.
north-alabama.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Danny, a guitar teacher; two kids who play in the school band. Hosts a listening party every Sunday.
gags: Reviews every game like an album.
Tells Terrell that a startup isn't a song.
Plays a different record before every home broadcast.
north-alabama.compassion: High. Credits everyone in the band, not just the frontman.
north-alabama.worldview: Everyone in the studio matters, and so does everyone on the team.

tarleton-state.bio: Bo Jennings grew up in Stephenville, rode bulls for five years and broke enough bones to retire before thirty. He edits The Stephenville Ledger and calls every Texans game like a rodeo from the Cowboy Capital, though he is still working out which events are basketball. He once tried to protest a loss to the rodeo office. No relation to the UC Davis Jennings, he says, though he'd like to meet him.
tarleton-state.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Stephenville, son of a dairy farmer and a church secretary; rodeo bull rider, then a feed salesman.
tarleton-state.beat: INVENTED. Called in rodeo results to the Ledger for years; when the sports editor quit, they gave him the basketball beat too, and he never noticed the difference.
tarleton-state.look: Purple and white hoodie with TARLETON across the front, short dark hair, wiry build, sunny grin (portrait).
tarleton-state.favorite: To research: a real Texans player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Abilene is a fine town if you like wind indoors.
Every win is a bull ride: eight seconds of holding on.
The rodeo office should handle basketball complaints.
tarleton-state.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Jess, a barrel racer; two kids and four horses. Still has every belt buckle he ever won.
gags: Calls every win 'roping it'.
Tells Wade the wind doesn't blow in the rodeo arena; Wade says it does.
Protests losses to the rodeo office.
tarleton-state.compassion: Big; helps every rancher in a jam.
tarleton-state.worldview: Cowboy Capital or not, everybody deserves a fair ride.

ut-arlington.bio: Rosa Treviño grew up in Arlington, worked ten years as a stadium operations manager for the big venues down the road and loves the little arena more than any of them. She edits The Arlington Courier and never lets anyone forget the small gym is the one with the heart. She is sharp, stylish and allergic to luxury suites. She knows where every bathroom is in every stadium in the Metroplex, and she will tell you which ones to avoid.
ut-arlington.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Arlington, daughter of an auto-plant worker and a hairdresser; stadium operations manager for ten years.
ut-arlington.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a Courier op-ed called 'The Little Arena That Could' and was hired as sports editor the next week.
ut-arlington.look: Blue and orange quarter-zip with UT ARLINGTON embroidered, brown hair pulled back, poised confident smile (portrait).
ut-arlington.favorite: To research: a real Mavericks player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Stephenville is a lovely town for people who think a rodeo is a personality.
The real show is never in the luxury suites.
The small gym has more heart per seat than any stadium in Texas.
ut-arlington.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Marco, a high school band director; two kids who play in the drumline. Runs a book club for stadium workers.
gags: Rates every arena by its bathrooms.
Tells Bo the rodeo isn't a sport, and he says the same about basketball.
Refuses to say the name of the big stadium down the road.
ut-arlington.compassion: High. Champions the workers behind the scenes.
ut-arlington.worldview: The people in the small rooms matter more than the people in the suites.

west-georgia.bio: Terrell Moss grew up in Carrollton, worked three years at an Atlanta startup that never shipped a product and came home to cover something that actually launches. He edits The Carrollton Mercury and frames the Wolves' Division I leap as a startup story, treating every win like a funding round. He is young, plugged in and endlessly optimistic. He has a pitch deck for every season and a slide for every loss he'd rather not show.
west-georgia.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Carrollton, son of a wire-plant worker and a teacher; product manager at an Atlanta startup for three years.
west-georgia.beat: INVENTED. Pitched the Mercury on a Wolves newsletter with a slide deck; the editor hired him after slide two.
west-georgia.look: Blue and red striped polo with WEST GEORGIA embroidered, short brown hair, clean-shaven, eager grin (portrait).
west-georgia.favorite: To research: a real Wolves player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Florence is a lovely town that should stop telling everyone about its records.
Every new program is a startup, and the Wolves are about to IPO.
A loss is just a quarter you leave off the slide deck.
west-georgia.off_air: INVENTED. Single; lives in a loft on the square. Runs a podcast about small-town startups with four listeners.
gags: Pitches every win like a funding round.
Tells Callie Mae that a record is just a legacy product.
Shows a slide deck on air for every big game.
west-georgia.compassion: Big; mentors high school kids on side projects.
west-georgia.humor: Jargon-heavy and self-aware; the joke is on him.
west-georgia.worldview: Small towns can build big things if everybody pitches in.

charleston-southern.bio: Lowell Grimes edits The North Charleston Compass and covers Charleston Southern basketball like a pirate story he heard once at a fish fry. He grew up in a shrimping family on the Cooper River, ran a seafood shack most of his adult life, and talked his way onto the desk by bringing frogmore stew to the press room. He loves the Buccaneers, Lowcountry cooking and saying arr at the wrong moment. His reading glasses have missed more big plays than most referees.
charleston-southern.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in a shrimping family off the Cooper River in North Charleston. Ran a seafood shack called The Leaky Galleon until the roof started agreeing with the name.
charleston-southern.beat: INVENTED. Brought frogmore stew to the press room every home game until somebody handed him a microphone to keep him busy. The Compass needed an editor and he was already sitting there.
charleston-southern.look: Navy polo with gold piping and CHARLESTON SOUTHERN on the chest, short graying hair, clean-shaven, easy grin (portrait).
charleston-southern.favorite: To research: a real Buccaneers player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Every Lowcountry problem can be solved with a boil, a folding table and newspaper for a tablecloth.
Rock Hill is a lovely town for people who don't need the ocean.
A Buccaneers team should press full court, because pirates board ships; they don't wait at the dock.
charleston-southern.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Darlene, who runs the shack now and makes the better hush puppies. Collects ship-in-a-bottle kits he has never once finished.
gags: Pats every pocket for his reading glasses while they sit on his head.
Translates the box score into pirate, badly.
Sends Royce a cooler of shrimp after every loss to Winthrop, labeled 'tribute.'
charleston-southern.temperament: Sunny and unhurried, like a tide that comes in when it feels like it.
charleston-southern.disposition: Generous, scatterbrained, delighted by almost everything.
charleston-southern.compassion: Feeds first, asks questions later; nobody leaves his table hungry.
charleston-southern.humor: Bumbling pirate dad; he's always the punchline and he knows it.
charleston-southern.worldview: A good town is one where the neighbors share a pot and a boat. Darlene explains the transfer portal to him twice a season.

gardner-webb.bio: Mary Beth Yount runs The Boiling Springs Sentinel out of a back room that smells like coffee and church cookbooks. She managed the elementary school cafeteria for years, which taught her to read a room of hungry people and grade them fairly. She covers the Runnin' Bulldogs the way she judges the Baptist potluck: effort first, presentation second. She knows most of town by first name and the rest by their casserole. Her Spartanburg rival insists he is from a bigger place. She lets him.
gardner-webb.backstory: INVENTED. Raised on a dairy farm outside Boiling Springs, the middle of five sisters. Managed the elementary school cafeteria and ran the potluck judging table at First Baptist.
gardner-webb.beat: INVENTED. Wrote such pointed letters to the editor about Bulldogs coverage that the retiring editor gave her the keys and the overdue printing bill.
gardner-webb.look: Red and black GARDNER-WEBB hoodie, shoulder-length brown hair, a polite smile that is still deciding about you (portrait).
gardner-webb.favorite: To research: a real Runnin' Bulldogs player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: A town this small can out-shout a city if it eats together first.
Spartanburg calls itself the Hub City because nobody else would.
A team that hustles back on defense gets an A, even if the jump shot looks like a dropped pie.
gardner-webb.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Dwayne, a quiet HVAC man who agrees with her in public. Keeps a ranked list of every banana pudding in Cleveland County.
gags: Scores each game on a potluck card: taste, effort, presentation, and whether you brought enough for everyone.
Says 'bless their hearts' and holds up fingers to show how much she means it.
Reminds Darius that the Hub City is a rest stop with ambition.
gardner-webb.temperament: Steady and observant, slow to boil, impossible to fool.
gardner-webb.appropriateness: PG. All shade, delivered with a casserole.
gardner-webb.compassion: Fierce. She'll roast your free throws and then drive your grandma to the doctor.
gardner-webb.humor: Dry small-town shade with perfect timing.
gardner-webb.worldview: Small places hold people up. She grades effort over polish because that's how her town gets by.
gardner-webb.rube: No. The desk's homegrown potluck judge.

high-point.bio: Jalen Pierce edits The High Point Examiner and reviews Panthers basketball like a sectional sofa at market week: fit, finish and whether it holds up when company comes over. He spent his twenties selling recliners in a showroom the size of an airport, which is where he learned to talk. He is sleek, quick and very certain about joinery. He once called a zone defense 'mid-century.' He still cannot explain what that meant, but he stands by it.
high-point.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in a High Point family that has delivered furniture for three generations. Sold recliners on the showroom floor during market weeks and became the guy everyone sent the indecisive customers to.
high-point.beat: INVENTED. Started a blog rating Panthers games like furniture, with stars for craftsmanship. The Examiner hired him when the blog outdrew its sports page.
high-point.look: Purple and white HIGH POINT quarter-zip, short brown hair, neatly trimmed beard, showroom smile (portrait).
high-point.favorite: To research: a real Panthers player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: A good half-court offense should have clean joints and no wobble.
Winthrop plays like a heavy oak hutch: sturdy, handsome and impossible to move.
Building a roster through the portal is just flat-pack furniture with better marketing.
high-point.off_air: INVENTED. Lives in a loft with one perfect armchair and no other seating. Has assembled a crib for his sister's baby three times and still has leftover screws.
gags: Inspects the underside of the press table before every broadcast.
Grades every possession on a scale from 'floor model' to 'heirloom.'
Tries to sell Royce a loveseat on air.
high-point.temperament: Bright and fast, a little too pleased with his own metaphors.
high-point.appropriateness: PG. Never swears, occasionally says 'veneer' like it's a curse.
high-point.compassion: Kind to everyone who has ever worked a retail floor, which is most people.
high-point.humor: Overcommitted metaphor guy; the joke is how far he'll take it.
high-point.worldview: Things made well and made to last are worth caring about, teams and towns included. Learning that not everything can be measured in thread count.

longwood.bio: Hattie Farmer taught fourth grade in Prince Edward County for most of her life and now edits The Farmville Lantern from a desk covered in red pens. She covers the Lancers with a teacher's eye: firm on effort, gentle with the kids, unforgiving about sloppy passing. She believes the bounce pass is the most honest play in basketball and writes small notes of praise to the best ones. She grades Longwood strictly and the visitors fairly, and she will show you the rubric.
longwood.backstory: INVENTED. Born on a tobacco farm outside Farmville, the daughter of a county extension agent. Taught fourth grade for decades and coached the girls' JV team on the side.
longwood.beat: INVENTED. Retired, got bored by the second Tuesday, and started grading Lancers games in the Lantern's letters section until the editor asked her to take the whole page.
longwood.look: Navy and gray LONGWOOD polo, chin-length brown bob, warm and slightly evaluative smile (portrait).
longwood.favorite: To research: a real Lancers player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: The bounce pass is a lost art and she intends to find it.
A Farmville January is good for the character and bad for the knees.
Radford's bagpipes are lovely and have never once boxed anyone out.
longwood.off_air: INVENTED. Widowed, with two grown sons who still hand in their holiday cards for her review. Gardens, walks the High Bridge trail, and keeps gold stars in her purse.
gags: Hands out written grades at halftime, with comments.
Writes thank-you notes to individual bounce passes.
Asks Ainsley to put the bagpipes away 'until she can share.'
longwood.temperament: Calm and gracious, with a dry edge like a porch in September.
longwood.compassion: Endless for young people; she remembers they are still learning.
longwood.humor: Bone-dry teacher wit, delivered without looking up from her notes.
longwood.worldview: Everybody can improve if somebody takes the time to show them how. Fundamentals are a form of respect.
longwood.rube: No. The desk's grader, and proud of it.

presbyterian.bio: Calvin Rhodes edits The Clinton Beacon and believes, with his whole chest, that the Blue Hose are the best small school in any big room. He was a youth minister in Clinton until the Beacon's sports editor retired and nobody else volunteered. He considers the Blue Hose name a gift and defends it to strangers in airports. He treats every win as proof that size is overrated and every loss as a clerical error. He has ordered more commemorative T-shirts than he has drawers.
presbyterian.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Clinton, son of a mill mechanic and a church organist. Spent a decade as a youth minister, running lock-ins and losing at dodgeball to seventh graders.
presbyterian.beat: INVENTED. Filled in on the Beacon's sports page for one weekend and simply never gave it back.
presbyterian.look: Royal blue and garnet PRESBYTERIAN hoodie, short dark hair, full trimmed beard, the face of a man about to tell you about his team (portrait).
presbyterian.favorite: To research: a real Blue Hose player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Blue Hose is the best nickname in America and he will debate anyone, Darius included, in a parking lot.
Small schools play harder because the whole town knows their names.
Every big-conference fan should have to ride a Big South bus once.
presbyterian.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Leah, a nurse who works nights and watches his broadcasts on replay at double speed. Coaches his daughter's rec team and argues every call with love.
gags: Orders a commemorative T-shirt after every win, exhibitions included.
Measures opposing players with a tape measure he cannot reach high enough to use.
Explains to Darius that hose are socks, and socks are noble.
presbyterian.temperament: Revved up and sincere, a pep rally that never ends.
presbyterian.disposition: Loyal past the point of reason, cheerful in defeat.
presbyterian.appropriateness: G. Youth-ministry clean; 'dadgum' is the ceiling.
presbyterian.compassion: Huge for underdogs, which is every team he loves.
presbyterian.humor: Overenthusiastic hype guy; he's the joke and he's fine with it.
presbyterian.worldview: Small things matter because people love them. Still learning that the other side's fans love their teams too.

radford.bio: Ainsley MacRae edits The Radford Register and covers Highlanders basketball with clan pride, a love of the New River and a pipe band she can summon on short notice. She spent her twenties guiding rafts and testing water quality for the county, which made her calm in rapids and impatient with excuses. She is crisp, wry and quick with a Scottish proverb she may have made up. Her rival in Farmville wants the bagpipes turned down. Ainsley wants them turned up.
radford.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Radford with a Scottish grandfather who played pipes at every wedding in the county. Guided whitewater trips on the New River, then worked as a water-quality tech.
radford.beat: INVENTED. Started bringing her grandfather's old pipe band to Highlanders games, wrote it up for the Register, and the column became a job.
radford.look: Red and white RADFORD quarter-zip, long straight brown hair, a bright confident smile (portrait).
radford.favorite: To research: a real Highlanders player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: The New River is older than the mountains around it, and Radford's patience is older than that.
Every home game should open with pipes, and the visiting team can bring a kazoo.
Longwood would be tougher if it ever had to paddle upstream.
radford.off_air: INVENTED. Lives with her partner Morgan and two border collies named Haggis and Ceilidh. Plays a mean tin whistle and a worse fiddle.
gags: Cues a pipe band for every lead change, whether or not one is available.
Translates rival scouting reports into clan feuds.
Offers Hattie earplugs in a decorative tartan pouch.
radford.temperament: Cool in a crisis, river-guide steady.
radford.disposition: Wry, proud, quick to laugh at herself.
radford.appropriateness: PG. Will say 'bloody' if the pipes are involved.
radford.compassion: Strong. Looks after the stragglers on every trip and every team.
radford.humor: Wry and theatrical, in a Scottish accent she does not have.
radford.worldview: Rivers and towns both work when everyone pulls the same direction. A clan is about who you take care of, not who you keep out.

usc-upstate.bio: Darius Lyles edits The Spartanburg Observer and calls Spartanburg the Hub City at every opportunity, including weddings. He managed a peach packing shed outside town for years and still grades games by ripeness. He believes all roads in South Carolina, and possibly the Southeast, lead back to the Upstate. He is smooth on camera and lost off it, and he has driven past his own exit while explaining the map. Boiling Springs is his favorite place to be smug about.
usc-upstate.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Spartanburg, son of a railroad brakeman, which he believes explains the whole Hub City thing. Ran a peach packing shed and gave every truck driver a lecture on local history.
usc-upstate.beat: INVENTED. Called the Observer to complain that its Spartans coverage undersold the Upstate. They told him to write it himself, so he did.
usc-upstate.look: Black polo with green piping and USC UPSTATE on the chest, short brown hair, clean-shaven, confident grin (portrait).
usc-upstate.favorite: To research: a real Spartans player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Georgia peaches are a marketing campaign; Upstate peaches are a lifestyle.
Boiling Springs is a lovely place to pass through on the way to Spartanburg.
Every Big South road trip should route through the Hub City, efficiency be darned.
usc-upstate.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Renee, who does the actual navigating. Has a peach tree in the backyard he talks to more than the dog.
gags: Gets lost driving to away games while explaining why Spartanburg is the center of everything.
Rates every win on ripeness, from 'green' to 'cobbler.'
Sends Mary Beth a peach basket with a map that ends at his house.
usc-upstate.temperament: Smooth and assured, especially when wrong.
usc-upstate.compassion: Kind and generous, quick to give a stranger directions, mostly bad ones.
usc-upstate.humor: Swagger that collapses on contact with reality; he's the joke.
usc-upstate.worldview: Home is the center of the map and everyone is welcome there. Renee keeps reminding him that other towns feel the same about theirs.
usc-upstate.rube: Yes: the lovable Hub City rube.

unc-asheville.bio: Fern Whitaker edits The Asheville Dispatch and reviews Bulldogs basketball like a gallery opening, with notes on composition, color and negative space. She threw pots in a riverside studio for years and taught ceramics to retirees who mostly wanted to talk. She saves her highest praise for ball movement and her sharpest words for a forced shot. She grades her own team as hard as anyone. She once gave a road win three stars because the second half lacked a thesis.
unc-asheville.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in a West Asheville family of bluegrass musicians and was the one who could not play anything. Ran a pottery studio and taught wheel-throwing classes on weeknights.
unc-asheville.beat: INVENTED. Wrote a review of a Bulldogs game for a gallery newsletter as a joke; the Dispatch reprinted it and asked for more.
unc-asheville.look: Royal blue and white UNC ASHEVILLE hoodie, graying brown hair pulled back, sun-lined face and an amused smile (portrait).
unc-asheville.favorite: To research: a real Bulldogs player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Five passes and a layup is finer art than most of what hangs downtown.
Boiling Springs grades basketball like a casserole; Asheville grades it like a canvas.
Mountain basketball is best watched with a view and a cup of something local.
unc-asheville.off_air: INVENTED. Lives with her wife Ruth and a studio cat named Glaze. Hikes the Parkway on Sundays and sketches the trees badly on purpose.
gags: Awards stars to individual possessions and hangs them in a little online gallery.
Describes a turnover as 'derivative.'
Invites Mary Beth to an opening every year; Mary Beth brings a casserole.
unc-asheville.temperament: Unhurried and observant, like someone waiting for the kiln to cool.
unc-asheville.disposition: Artsy, sharp-eyed, generous with praise when it's earned.
unc-asheville.compassion: Deep. Believes every player is a work in progress and says so.
unc-asheville.humor: Arch critic's deadpan, punctured by her own pretension.
unc-asheville.worldview: Beauty is in the cooperation, on a canvas or a court. She notices who did the unseen work.

winthrop.bio: Royce Bynum edits The Rock Hill Courant and treats every Winthrop game like Sunday dinner with company. He ran a downtown drugstore with a lunch counter for most of his career and still holds the door for anyone in sight. He grades wins on manners and losses on free throws, which he considers a matter of character. He is courtly, gentle and very certain about the proper way to shoot one. He has never fully understood the shot clock and has made his peace with that.
winthrop.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Rock Hill to a textile mill family, he became a pharmacist and ran a downtown drugstore with a lunch counter and the town's best limeade.
winthrop.beat: INVENTED. Retired, began writing gentlemanly letters to the Courant about Eagles free throw shooting, and was eventually invited to stop writing letters and start writing columns.
winthrop.look: Garnet and gold WINTHROP quarter-zip over a collared shirt, short gray hair, a polite, weathered half smile (portrait).
winthrop.favorite: To research: a real Eagles player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: A missed free throw is a small failure of character, forgivable but noted.
Sweet tea at the door is the minimum standard of hospitality for a visiting team.
Gardner-Webb has lovely manners and questionable free throw mechanics.
winthrop.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Eugenia for decades; she handles the remote and most of the opinions. Shoots underhand free throws in his driveway every Sunday after church.
gags: Demonstrates the proper underhand free throw on air, using a dinner roll.
Calls the shot clock 'that nervous little box.'
Sends Mary Beth handwritten condolence cards after Gardner-Webb losses.
winthrop.temperament: Courtly and patient, with a pharmacist's precision.
winthrop.appropriateness: G. Says 'my stars' at the very most.
winthrop.compassion: Old-school kindness; remembers your mother's name and your prescription.
winthrop.humor: Fussy-gentleman comedy; the joke is how seriously he takes a free throw.
winthrop.worldview: Good manners are a way of saying everyone counts. Learning, slowly, that the game sped up without asking him.

eastern-illinois.bio: Dana Kohler grew up in the bleachers of a Coles County gym where her father coached high school ball, and she has been counting rebounds ever since. She worked as a physical therapist in Charleston before taking over The Charleston Spectator. She is brisk, fair and allergic to excuses, and she grades the Panthers by who won the glass. In her house, winning the boards and winning the game are the same sentence. She once boxed out a man at a buffet without meaning to.
eastern-illinois.backstory: INVENTED. Daughter of a small-town high school coach in Coles County, she grew up keeping his stat book. Worked as a physical therapist, mostly rehabbing knees from rec-league basketball.
eastern-illinois.beat: INVENTED. Sent the Spectator a rebounding chart after every Panthers game for two seasons until they printed one, then hired her to make it every week.
eastern-illinois.look: Royal blue and gray EASTERN ILLINOIS polo, shoulder-length brown hair, focused gaze and a slight, knowing smile (portrait).
eastern-illinois.favorite: To research: a real Panthers player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Rebounding margin is the most honest number in basketball.
Macomb is far from the interstate because nobody goes there by accident.
Central Illinois winters build rebounders; nobody gives up position in a snowdrift.
eastern-illinois.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Tom, a seed salesman, with two teenage sons who have learned never to leave a loose ball. Runs a half-marathon every spring and boxes out at the water stations.
gags: Puts the rebounding margin on screen before the final score.
Boxes out anyone near the snack table.
Sends Jess a road atlas every Christmas with the interstate highlighted.
eastern-illinois.temperament: Brisk and businesslike; warms up by the second half.
eastern-illinois.appropriateness: PG. A clipped 'come on' is her loudest outburst.
eastern-illinois.compassion: Practical and steady; fixes your knee and then your attitude.
eastern-illinois.worldview: Effort is measurable and everyone deserves credit for theirs. Fair to the other side, always.

lindenwood.bio: Mike Brandt edits The St. Charles Register and believes every Lions win deserves a parade down Main Street, permit or no permit. He worked the fryer at his uncle's Italian place for years, where he perfected toasted ravioli and lost several notebooks. He is brand-new to Division I coverage and thrilled about all of it. He makes a bold prediction before every game and then cannot find where he wrote it. Andre at SIUE keeps the receipts. Mike keeps the ravioli.
lindenwood.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in St. Charles above his uncle's Italian restaurant and worked the line from high school on. Has fried more toasted ravioli than anyone in the county, by his own count.
lindenwood.beat: INVENTED. Ran the Register's food column until Lindenwood moved up to Division I, then volunteered for basketball because the press room had a microwave.
lindenwood.look: Black hoodie with LINDENWOOD in gold across the chest, short dark hair, clean-shaven, a big-plans smile (portrait).
lindenwood.favorite: To research: a real Lions player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Every Division I win for Lindenwood should be a city holiday.
Toasted ravioli is the official snack of the Ohio Valley, whether the league knows it or not.
Edwardsville is a fine town in Illinois, which is a state he can almost see from here.
lindenwood.off_air: INVENTED. Married to Angela, who keeps a folder of his lost predictions. Coaches his son's T-ball team and draws plays on napkins.
gags: Announces a pregame prediction, then can't find the napkin he wrote it on.
Asks City Hall for a parade permit after every win.
Brings Andre a tray of toasted ravioli as a peace offering and eats most of it himself.
lindenwood.temperament: Excitable and sunny, a golden retriever with a press pass.
lindenwood.appropriateness: PG. 'Holy cannoli' is as rough as it gets.
lindenwood.compassion: Feeds everyone, forgives everything, especially his own team.
lindenwood.humor: Lovable mess; the joke is on him and he laughs first.
lindenwood.worldview: New things deserve a celebration and so do the people who show up for them. Andre is teaching him what a possession is.
lindenwood.rube: Yes: the lovable Main Street rube.

morehead-state.bio: Opal Caudill edits The Morehead Ledger from a desk that faces the hills she grew up in. She was a home health nurse in Rowan County for most of her career, driving switchbacks to check on folks who would not come into town. She trusts defense, toughness and any team that works for a living. She does not dress up a bad night, and she does not let anyone else dress one down. Her grandchildren call her during games for scouting reports.
morehead-state.backstory: INVENTED. Raised in a holler outside Morehead, the daughter of a coal truck driver and a schoolteacher. Spent her career as a home health nurse on back roads.
morehead-state.beat: INVENTED. Called in to a local radio show so often about Eagles defense that the station gave her a segment; the Ledger started running the transcripts.
morehead-state.look: Navy and gold MOREHEAD STATE quarter-zip, shoulder-length blonde hair, a steady, appraising look (portrait).
morehead-state.favorite: To research: a real Eagles player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: Defense is honest work and the scoreboard is the paycheck.
Southern Indiana is still learning that Division I is a job, not a party.
A team from the hills will outlast a team from the flatlands in February.
morehead-state.off_air: INVENTED. Widowed, with a pile of grandchildren and a quilting circle that doubles as a scouting department. Cans green beans and grudges in equal amounts.
gags: Gives every Eagles defender a 'shift report' at halftime.
Calls Clint 'the new boy' no matter how long Southern Indiana has been in the league.
Keeps a grandchild on the phone at all times for a second opinion.
morehead-state.disposition: Tough, warm underneath, no patience for show.
morehead-state.appropriateness: G. 'Well, I never' is her cussing.
morehead-state.compassion: Deep and practical; she shows up with soup before you know you're sick.
morehead-state.worldview: Work is dignity, and people in small places deserve to be seen doing it. She respects anybody who gives an honest effort.

siue.bio: Andre Whitlow edits The Edwardsville Observer and covers the Cougars with a laptop full of possession data and strong feelings about pace. He was a statistics grad student until he noticed he spent more time charting fast breaks than writing his thesis. He is young, quick and analytically sharp, and nearly helpless at anything that will not fit in a spreadsheet. He has never successfully parallel parked. He tracks Mike's forgotten Lindenwood predictions as a public service.
siue.backstory: INVENTED. Grew up in Edwardsville, son of two accountants who kept the family budget in color-coded binders. Spent his grad-school years charting Cougars possessions instead of his thesis data.
siue.beat: INVENTED. His possession-by-possession blog became the most-read thing in town that wasn't a school closing; the Observer hired him before he could start a rival paper.
siue.look: Red and black SIUE polo, short brown hair, clean-shaven, earnest young face (portrait).
siue.favorite: To research: a real Cougars player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: A team that walks the ball up the floor is leaving free points on the table.
Lindenwood's predictions should be tracked by a neutral third party, and he volunteers.
The fast break is the purest expression of trust in basketball.
siue.off_air: INVENTED. Lives with two roommates and a whiteboard. Can recite the pace of every OVC team but forgets to eat lunch.
gags: Charts the pace of the postgame handshake line.
Keeps a public spreadsheet of Mike's lost predictions, with a confidence interval.
Tries to explain expected points to his grandmother, who wins the argument.
siue.temperament: Quick and keyed up, a stopwatch in human form.
siue.disposition: Earnest, nerdy, sweetly oblivious off the court.
siue.appropriateness: G. Says 'oh, come on' to bad shot selection.
siue.compassion: Kind and patient with people who don't like numbers, mostly.
siue.humor: Nerd comedy; the joke is how little the spreadsheet helps him in real life.
siue.worldview: Good systems help everybody, on a court or in a town. Learning that some things only make sense if you're there in person.

southeast-missouri.bio: Bonnie Kasten edits The Cape Girardeau Chronicle and checks the Mississippi River gauge before she checks the box score. She dispatched towboats for years and learned that everything rises and falls, usually when you have plans. She covers the Redhawks with a river-town realist's eye and a quick wit. A good win is steady water. A bad loss is a low-water night that will come back up. Buck in Martin wants a parade float for every win. Bonnie wants him to check the forecast first.
southeast-missouri.backstory: INVENTED. Born in Cape Girardeau to a family of river pilots and a grandmother who ran a bait shop under the bridge. Dispatched towboats for a barge line until her eyes got tired of radar.
southeast-missouri.beat: INVENTED. Began adding a Redhawks line to her river-stage reports for the boat crews; the Chronicle noticed the crews were reading them for the basketball.
southeast-missouri.look: Red and black SEMO hoodie, chin-length brown bob, a knowing, skeptical smile (portrait).
southeast-missouri.favorite: To research: a real Redhawks player or era they can champion, with a source.
hot_takes: You can tell everything about a town by how it talks about its river.
Martin's Soybean Festival is a fine party for a town that's never had to sandbag.
A basketball season is like the river: wait long enough and it comes back.
